defaults.permitted_development: A modest porch on a dwellinghouse in Scotland is usually permitted development if its footprint does not exceed 3 square metres, no part is higher than 3m and it stays more than 2m from any boundary with a road, provided no local restriction has removed the right.

rules.height_rules: The key Scottish height limit is 3m overall. There is no extra allowance for a pitched or feature porch roof once the structure passes that level.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance. The key size test is footprint, which should not exceed 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: No part of the porch should be within 2m of a boundary with a road. There are no ordinary porch rights in a conservation area, so location matters as much as size.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance beyond the overall footprint and 3m height limit. The roof form must stay within those national thresholds.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that fit the dwellinghouse and its setting. Listed building consent or heritage controls can still apply even where the porch dimensions are small.

rules.permitted_development: Scottish Class 1C can often cover a porch where the footprint is no more than 3 square metres, the overall height is no more than 3m and the structure is more than 2m from the boundary with a road.

rules.height_rules: Porch height is capped at 3m overall in Scotland. A pitched roof, canopy or decorative form does not create a separate allowance beyond that maximum.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not assessed by a standalone projection figure. The controlling size limit is the overall footprint of 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: The 2m road-boundary rule is often the critical Scottish test on tight plots. Also remember that porches in conservation areas fall outside the ordinary Class 1C right.
rules.roof_rules: Roof design is secondary to the small-porch limits: the whole structure must still stay within 3 square metres and 3m in height. Canopy-heavy designs can fail even where the enclosed space looks modest.
rules.materials_rules: The best porch designs usually look like a natural extension of the entrance rather than a bolt-on box. Matching or carefully complementary materials often matter most on the front elevation.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Scotland, conservation area status can narrow normal householder permitted development rights for visible external work. Check local authority guidance before relying on national allowances.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent is required in Scotland for demolition, extension or material alteration of a listed building, inside or out, where character is affected.
restrictions.article4_notes: No borough-wide Article 4 note is recorded here, but site-specific directions or planning conditions can still remove permitted development rights on particular properties.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, a small porch can normally use the ordinary householder route when it stays within the 3 square metre footprint, 3m height and road-boundary separation limits.

rules.height_rules: Whatever roof form you choose, the porch should stay within a 3m overall height cap.
rules.depth_rules: Porches do not get a dedicated projection allowance in Scotland. The practical size test is that the footprint must stay at or below 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: Check the road boundary first. On many front elevations, the porch dimensions may be fine but the required 2m separation to a road boundary, together with conservation area status, is what determines the answer.
rules.roof_rules: A porch roof does not get its own Scottish allowance. The overall porch, including any projecting canopy, still has to fit within the 3 square metre and 3m limits.
rules.materials_rules: Because porches are usually prominent from the street, external materials and detailing should sit comfortably with the house. Sensitive Scottish settings often call for the most restrained finish.

rules.boundary_rules: Check the road boundary first. On many front elevations, the porch dimensions may be fine but the required 2m separation to a road boundary, together with conservation area status, is what determines the answer.
rules.roof_rules: A porch roof does not get its own Scottish allowance. The overall porch, including any projecting canopy, still has to fit within the 3 square metre and 3m limits.
rules.materials_rules: Because porches are usually prominent from the street, external materials and detailing should sit comfortably with the house. Sensitive Scottish settings often call for the most restrained finish.

rules.permitted_development: A modest porch on a dwellinghouse in Scotland is usually permitted development if its footprint does not exceed 3 square metres, no part is higher than 3m and it stays more than 2m from any boundary with a road, provided no local restriction has removed the right.

rules.height_rules: The key Scottish height limit is 3m overall. There is no extra allowance for a pitched or feature porch roof once the structure passes that level.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance. The key size test is footprint, which should not exceed 3 square metres.
rules.boundary_rules: No part of the porch should be within 2m of a boundary with a road. There are no ordinary porch rights in a conservation area, so location matters as much as size.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance beyond the overall footprint and 3m height limit. The roof form must stay within those national thresholds.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials that fit the dwellinghouse and its setting. Listed building consent or heritage controls can still apply even where the porch dimensions are small.
